approach.mission_intro_html: The Foundation runs programs for teachers and coordinators, and equip them with mentors and funding.Yes, monthly stipend
mission: More than half of every program is practice. The toolkit is curated: an inquiry stance, structured discussion formats, classroom craft, mentored practice with real children.
We don’t have a new pedagogy to sell, and want it to work<br class="desktop-break"> in a regular class of 35 on a Tuesday morning.
Decades of research on teacher development agree on this. What changes classrooms isn’t lecture hours — it’s standards, coaching, and teachers learning together.

fellowship.title_html: dear teachers,
intro: You see the results of years of classroom disruption better than anyone, and you’ve been left to face it alone. We want to give you tools, time and backing — and the respect your work deserves.
We work where the leverage is highest: the late primary and early middle school years, before motivation fades. Joining our fellowship would give you:

benefits.title: Crash-course into the hardest parts of the craft
benefits.body: Intensives where we explore and try specific teaching practices, then several weeks of teaching children, with a weekly mentor debrief
questions: “how do you build motivation that doesn’t depend on grades?”
“how do you start a lesson with a real question?”
“how do you get a class’s attention without raising your voice?”

benefits.title: Weekly mentorship sessions
benefits.body: For the reflection and lessons that go sideways.

benefits.title: Participant’s stipend
benefits.body: You have more than enough work without us, so we pay participants a stipend — both for the training and for the practice with children.

leaders.title_html:
dear school
leaders,
intro: Strong teachers need schools where they can do good work and want to stay. That’s why we want to work not only with teachers, but also for people who shape the teams around them.
In fall 2026, we’re launching a pilot program, where we’ll focus on:

results: In summer 2026, 17 teachers finished our first intensive. 16 of them are now continuing paid teaching practice with children and meet with a mentor every week; 14 of the 17 would recommend the program to colleagues.
Two-thirds of the children we surveyed said they’d like to have lessons like these at school.
That’s encouraging, but it’s still a small, unusually friendly setting. We’ll be much more convinced if the same thing happens in ordinary classrooms.
